item.title: Optics Notes#3: Scalar waves
item.dc:creator: Qi Huang
item.description:
We briefly examine the simplest solution of this equation.

Plane waves

A plane wave is a wave whose amplitude is constant on every plane perpendicular to a fixed propagation direction. The field can therefore change as we move along the direction of propagation, but it has the same value at all points on one such plane.

Let be a unit vector in the fixed propagation direction, and let be the position vector of a point . The scalar measures the position of along . We denote this coordinate by .

This form expresses the defining property of a plane wave: the field depends on position only through , rather than on the three Cartesian coordinates independently. Consequently, all points satisfying have the same value of at a fixed time. These points form a plane whose normal is .

Because depends on , , and only through the single variable , its Cartesian derivatives can be found by the chain rule. For example, changing changes at the rate , which gives

Applying the same relation twice gives the second derivatives. Since is a fixed vector, its components are constants and can be taken outside the derivatives.

The unit-vector condition is what reduces the three-dimensional Laplacian to a one-dimensional second derivative along the propagation direction. The wave equation therefore becomes

To solve this one-dimensional equation, introduce the characteristic variables

The variables and move in opposite directions when time increases. They are useful because the wave equation separates naturally into a part depending only on and a part depending only on . Substituting these derivatives into the reduced wave equation, the terms involving only and only cancel, leaving

This condition says that the -dependent and -dependent parts are independent of one another. Integrating with respect to the two variables gives the general solution

Here represents a disturbance propagated with velocity in the positive direction, while represents a disturbance propagated with the same speed in the negative direction. A plane wave travelling in only one direction is obtained by setting the other function to zero.

Spherical waves

A spherical wave has spherical wavefronts centered on the source. Its amplitude is the same at every point on a sphere of radius , so the field depends on position only through the distance from the source, rather than through the direction of . We consider the region , away from the source itself. Here . Since depends on all three Cartesian coordinates, the derivatives of can again be obtained with the chain rule. The factor is the directional derivative of the radial coordinate with respect to . It is the -component of the unit vector pointing away from the source. The corresponding expressions for the and derivatives are obtained by cyclic permutation of the coordinates. Adding the three second derivatives gives the Laplacian for a spherically symmetric field: The first term describes the change in the radial slope as the spherical surface expands, while the second term is the ordinary second derivative in the radial direction. The expression can be simplified by introducing the product . Thus the three-dimensional Laplacian has been reduced to a one-dimensional second derivative of . Substituting this result into the scalar wave equation gives Multiplying by and using the fact that is independent of time, the equation for has exactly the same form as the one-dimensional plane-wave equation. We can therefore replace by and by in the previous solution: The first term is an outward-propagating spherical wave and the second is an inward-propagating one. The factor expresses the geometric spreading of the wave: as the radius increases, the same disturbance is distributed over a larger spherical surface, so its amplitude decreases.

Harmonic waves. The phase velocity

Harmonic waves

A fixed point sees the wave disturbance as a function of time only: For a periodic disturbance, the simplest important case is the sinusoidal function The quantities introduced in this expression are collected below.

Concept Definition Meaning
Fixed-point disturbance At a fixed position, the disturbance depends only on time.
Periodic disturbance The disturbance repeats after every period .
Amplitude The maximum value of the disturbance.
Phase The instantaneous position of the oscillation within one cycle.
Initial phase The phase at .
Angular frequency The phase change per unit time, measured in radians per second.
Period The time required for one complete vibration.
Frequency The number of complete vibrations per second.
Harmonic wave A wave whose time dependence is sinusoidal.

For a plane wave travelling in the direction of the unit vector with speed , replace by the retarded time . This gives The quantities describing its spatial variation are summarized in the following table.

Concept Definition Meaning
Plane harmonic wave A harmonic wave travelling in the direction .
Wavelength The distance over which the phase changes by .
Refractive index The ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium.
Reduced wavelength The wavelength of a wave with the same frequency in vacuum.
Wave number The number of wavelengths in vacuum per unit length.
Vacuum wave number The phase change per unit length in vacuum.
Medium wave number The phase change per unit length in the medium.
Wave vectors and Vectors pointing in the propagation direction, with magnitudes and .

Complex amplitudes

A plane wave has constant amplitude on each wavefront. More generally, a real time-harmonic wave can have both amplitude and phase varying with position: Here and are real scalar functions of position.

Concept Definition Meaning
Time-harmonic wave A real wave with a single angular frequency .
Amplitude function Determines how the amplitude varies from point to point.
Phase function Determines the phase at different positions.
Constant-amplitude surfaces Surfaces on which the amplitude is the same.
Cophasal surfaces or wave surfaces Surfaces on which the phase is the same.
Inhomogeneous wave Constant-amplitude surfaces do not generally coincide with cophasal surfaces. A wave whose amplitude and phase vary independently in space.

To separate the time dependence from the spatial dependence, introduce a complex representative and take its real part at the end: The function is the complex amplitude. It contains both the position-dependent amplitude and the position-dependent phase: Indeed, so this complex representation gives exactly the real wave introduced above. The advantage is that differentiation with respect to time becomes multiplication by .

Because does not depend on position, the spatial derivatives act only on : The time derivatives are Substituting these expressions into the scalar wave equation gives Since , it can be cancelled: Using and , this becomes the Helmholtz equation For the plane wave, the spatial phase function is

Phase velocity

Unlike a plane harmonic wave, a general time-harmonic wave need not be periodic in space. Its phase is , and a cophasal surface is defined by . To find how fast this surface advances, compare two nearby points on the same surface: Let be the unit vector in the direction of , and write . The speed in this direction is therefore The cophasal surface advances normally to itself. Thus is chosen parallel to , and the phase velocity is For a plane wave, and . Hence If , this can also be written as . In a non-dispersive medium, this phase velocity is the constant speed appearing in the scalar wave equation; for a more general wave, it may vary from point to point.

Wave packets. The group velocity

An exactly monochromatic wave is an idealization. By the Fourier theorem, a sufficiently regular wave can be represented as a superposition of monochromatic waves with different frequencies: In complex notation, the same decomposition is written as A wave is almost monochromatic when its Fourier amplitudes are appreciable only in a narrow frequency interval: To see how a wave packet is formed, consider two waves with nearby frequencies and wave numbers: Introducing the mean frequency and mean wave number, the superposition becomes This factorization follows from with and . The sum of the two waves therefore separates into a slowly varying factor and a rapidly varying carrier.

Source: Scalar waves

In panel (a), the blue curve is the carrier wave In panel (b), the red dashed curves are the positive and negative envelopes: The blue curve is the real wave inside these envelopes. In complex notation it is represented by and the plotted physical wave is its real part, The cosine factor is a slowly varying envelope, while the exponential factor is the rapidly oscillating carrier. The envelope maxima satisfy so the envelope moves with This limiting value is the group velocity. It describes the motion of the wave packet or envelope, whereas the carrier moves with the phase velocity . In a dispersive medium, these two velocities are generally different.

One-dimensional and three-dimensional wave groups

The one-dimensional result extends to a general three-dimensional wave. The intermediate steps are as follows.

For the one-dimensional case, start from a narrow band of frequencies and write Taking as the mean frequency and , factor out the mean oscillation: where the slowly varying complex amplitude is The amplitude of the wave group is determined by . Because may be complex, its squared magnitude is obtained by multiplying it by its complex conjugate: The star means complex conjugation: changes to , and each coefficient is replaced by . Thus is not a second physical wave; it is used to obtain the real, non-negative quantity .

The three-dimensional derivation has the same structure: where Multiplying by the conjugate gives For a narrow frequency interval, so the envelope depends mainly on This is the three-dimensional analogue of the one-dimensional envelope coordinate .

The resulting quantities can be compared as follows.

Quantity One-dimensional case Three-dimensional case
Complex representation
Constant-amplitude surface
Group velocity
Phase velocity
Main difference The wave varies along one spatial coordinate . The amplitude and phase vary throughout space, so gradients determine the propagation direction and speed.

In the three-dimensional case, the group velocity is normal to the constant-amplitude surface. When the wave depends only on , the gradient reduces to an ordinary derivative and the three-dimensional expression becomes the one-dimensional result.

This note explains how to derive Maxwell’s wave equations.

The wave equation

The Maxwell equations describe the electric and magnetic fields as a coupled system. The purpose of this note is to combine them into a single equation for one field. Once this is done, the propagation of light appears directly as a wave phenomenon.

We first record two vector identities that will be used below. For a vector field, the double curl can be written in terms of its divergence and Laplacian:

The second identity is the product rule for the curl. Here is a scalar field and is a vector field:

The first identity handles the geometry of the vector field. The second becomes important when the material parameters vary from point to point, because and can no longer be moved through a spatial derivative.

item.title: Scalar waves
item.description:
Wave packets

This figure shows a simple harmonic wave and the wave group formed by two nearby waves. The upper panel contains the carrier wave, while the lower panel contains the wave group and its positive and negative envelopes.

For two nearby waves, the wave group can be written schematically as

Parameters and wave functions

The following code defines the spatial grid and evaluates the carrier, envelope, and wave group at a chosen time.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


a = 1.0

omega_bar = 8.0       # central angular frequency
k_bar = 8.0           # central wave number

delta_omega = 0.8     # frequency difference
delta_k = 0.8         # wave-number difference

# Use x as a generic coordinate: t (or z).
x = np.linspace(0, 8 * np.pi, 2500)


def calculate_waves(x):
    """Calculate the carrier, envelope, and wave group along x."""

    phase = omega_bar * x
    envelope_phase = 0.5 * delta_omega * x

    carrier = a * np.cos(phase)
    envelope = 2 * a * np.cos(envelope_phase)
    wave_group = envelope * np.cos(phase)

    return carrier, envelope, wave_group

Initial state

The static figure below is the PNG output embedded in the article. It contains no Plotly or animation data.

carrier, envelope, wave_group = calculate_waves(x)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    2,
    1,
    figsize=(9, 5.6),
    sharex=True,
    gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [0.38, 0.62]},
)

# (a) Simple harmonic wave
axes[0].plot(x, carrier, color="#1f77b4", linewidth=1.5)
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"$V$")
axes[0].set_ylim(-1.35, 1.55)
axes[0].set_yticks([-a, 0, a])
axes[0].set_yticklabels([r"$-a$", r"$0$", r"$a$"])
axes[0].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
axes[0].text(0.985, 0.88, "(a)", transform=axes[0].transAxes, ha="right")

# (b) Wave group and envelopes
axes[1].plot(x, wave_group, color="#1f77b4", linewidth=1.2)
axes[1].plot(x, envelope, color="#d62728", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)
axes[1].plot(x, -envelope, color="#d62728", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2)
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"$t$ (or $z$)")
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$V$")
axes[1].set_ylim(-2.3, 2.45)
axes[1].set_yticks([-2 * a, -a, 0, a, 2 * a])
axes[1].set_yticklabels([r"$-2a$", r"$-a$", r"$0$", r"$a$", r"$2a$"])
axes[1].axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.7)
axes[1].text(0.985, 0.98, "(b)", transform=axes[1].transAxes, ha="right", va="top")

for axis in axes:
    axis.set_xlim(x.min(), x.max())
    axis.grid(False)

# Put x-axis ticks at the envelope zeros.
envelope_zero_positions = (2 * np.arange(10) + 1) * np.pi / delta_omega
envelope_zero_positions = envelope_zero_positions[
    envelope_zero_positions <= x.max()
]

x_ticks = np.concatenate(([0], envelope_zero_positions))
x_labels = [r"$0$"] + [
    rf"$\frac{{{2 * i + 1}\pi}}{{\delta\omega}}$"
    for i in range(len(envelope_zero_positions))
]
axes[1].set_xticks(x_ticks)
axes[1].set_xticklabels(x_labels)
for tick in axes[1].get_xticklabels():
    tick.set_fontsize(12)
    tick.set_fontweight("bold")

# The distance between adjacent envelope zeros is 2*pi/delta_omega.
axes[1].text(
    0.5,
    -0.28,
    r"adjacent zeros: $\frac{2\pi}{\delta\omega}$ (or $\frac{2\pi}{\delta k}$)",
    transform=axes[1].transAxes,
    ha="center",
    va="top",
    fontsize=9,
)

fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0.06, 1, 1])
plt.show()
